observation.visible_scene: A bright blue daytime sky dominated by a single large, backlit cumulus cloud near the center, its upper rim glowing white where the sun sits just behind it and produces a bright halo with a faint diagonal lens-flare streak. A leafy tree silhouette occupies the lower-right corner, thin power lines and a small insulator cross the bottom edge, and a lower, smaller cloud bank sits at the left. The camera is pointed upward at the sky.
visible_changes: Over the ~2.7 s excerpt every element in the frame—the central cloud, the sun's glare above it, the lower-left cloud, the tree, and the power lines—drifts slowly and uniformly downward by a similar amount, so their positions relative to one another stay fixed; this consistent co-movement of foreground and cloud indicates a slight upward camera tilt/pan rather than the cloud translating across the sky.

The sun's halo and the diagonal flare streak just above the cloud top subtly change brightness and spread (the streak appears to soften) while the glow keeps a constant offset from the cloud's upper edge, i.e. the glare does not move relative to the cloud.
The cloud's outline and internal puffy texture show no clear deformation, growth, or dissipation within the excerpt; the bright 'silver lining' rim remains in the same place on the cloud.
The tree branches and power lines remain static in shape, only shifting in frame position along with the rest of the scene.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the slow downward drift of the frame continues, reverses, or stops after the excerpt ends.
Any actual evolution of the cumulus cloud before or after this segment.
The true motion of the sun and the cause of the flare-streak change (camera angle vs. atmospheric effect).
uncertain_details: Exact nature and magnitude of the camera motion (tilt vs. pan vs. a very slight zoom) cannot be pinned down from the background alone.
Whether any minute cloud deformation is present or the shape is perfectly constant is hard to judge at this frame rate.
The relative positions of cloud, tree, and lines are stable, but small measurement-level shifts make a tiny independent cloud drift impossible to fully rule out.
